strengths: Soundness: The attention-mixture decomposition in Section 2 and Appendix A provides a convincing foundation for jointly matching local attention outputs and attention mass. The scalar bias correction addresses a real deficiency of simple token deletion: retained tokens otherwise systematically underrepresent the compacted block’s mass.

Originality: The contribution is a useful formulation of cache compaction as per-head attention matching, combining key selection, mass correction, and value fitting. Although the numerical subroutines are established, their combination provides a meaningful alternative to expensive end-to-end latent-cache optimization.

Significance: Figure 3 shows substantial improvements over token-pruning baselines across three model families and two benchmarks, especially at aggressive compaction ratios. Figure 1 demonstrates a compelling compaction-time advantage over the evaluated Cartridges configuration.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript clearly develops the motivation and method, and the appendices provide prompts, baseline adaptations, solver choices, numerical precision, and chunking details. The ablations distinguish the contributions of fitted values, biases, query generation, and head budgets.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly acknowledges slower OMP variants, weaker results than Cartridges at extreme compression, and unfinished inference-engine integration. The online AIME experiment is appropriately presented as preliminary. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described benchmark-based work.
weaknesses: Soundness and presentation: Claims that the construction is entirely closed-form and avoids gradient descent do not accurately describe Appendix C.2. OMP uses unconstrained least squares followed by clipping, while HighestAttnKeys uses two projected-gradient steps; neither generally solves NNLS exactly. Moreover, Appendix A’s per-query rescaling changes the least-squares weighting relative to the stated unnormalized mass objective. These are plausible practical approximations, but the actual optimized objective and solver guarantees should be stated accurately.

Reproducibility: Nonuniform head allocation is the most influential component in Figure 4, yet its calibration protocol is insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not clearly identify a disjoint calibration/evaluation split, fully specify the sensitivity-curve measurement procedure and allocation step size, or report calibration cost. The claimed reusable schedule would be more convincing with explicit held-out transfer results and released schedules.

Evaluation reliability: Main accuracy results lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics despite stochastic decoding. LongHealth contains only four independently compacted contexts, so 400 questions do not establish broad context-level robustness. Cartridges is evaluated on 20 QuALITY articles while other methods use 50; Appendix B.2 reports different full-cache accuracies for these sets. A matched-subset comparison and context-level confidence intervals are needed for precise superiority claims.

Practical significance: The paper measures compaction latency but not end-to-end decoding throughput, peak working memory, or amortization over subsequent requests. Gemma’s reported ratios apply only to global-attention layers, excluding unchanged sliding-window caches. Consequently, nominal compaction ratios should not be read as equivalent total-memory savings. The extrapolation to much larger models based on KV dimensions alone also omits the model-size dependence of reference-query generation.

Algorithm specification: Algorithm 2 loops for t iterations while selecting k keys per iteration, producing up to kt keys rather than the stated budget t. Algorithm 1’s unnormalized correlation criterion also does not generally select the column giving the largest residual reduction, as the accompanying text claims. These discrepancies should be corrected so the pseudocode unambiguously reproduces the evaluated methods.

strengths: Soundness: The core formulation is well motivated. Section 2 and Appendix A correctly explain why preserving both a block’s locally normalized attention output and its attention mass preserves its contribution when concatenated with other tokens, for queries where matching holds. The scalar biases address a concrete deficiency of unweighted token eviction.

Originality and significance: Combining attention-mass fitting, value reconstruction, and sparse key selection provides a useful alternative to expensive end-to-end cache optimization. Although the individual numerical tools are established, their application to this compaction objective offers a meaningful contribution beyond simply ranking and retaining tokens.

Empirical evidence: Figure 3 shows substantial improvements over pruning and summarization across three model families and two datasets, particularly at aggressive compaction ratios. The inclusion of a hybrid sliding-window model, component ablations, and reference-query comparisons strengthens the evidence. Figure 1 supports a substantial compaction-time advantage over the evaluated Cartridges configuration.

Presentation, reproducibility, and limitations: The paper generally explains the method clearly and supplies substantial implementation detail, baseline adaptations, prompts, and numerical settings. It explicitly acknowledges slower OMP variants, cases where Cartridges performs better, and unfinished inference-engine integration. The online-compaction experiment is appropriately presented as preliminary. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness of the optimization claims: The main text overstates the extent to which the method is closed-form and avoids gradient descent. Appendix C.2 uses clamped unconstrained least squares for OMP and two projected-gradient steps for highest-attention selection; neither generally solves NNLS exactly. Moreover, the per-query feature rescaling in Appendix A.2 changes the relative weighting of residuals in the stated mass-fitting objective. These are reasonable implementation choices, but the paper should distinguish the implemented approximation from the claimed optimizer and quantify the resulting fitting error.

Evaluation uncertainty: LongHealth contains only four aggregated contexts, and the main accuracy comparisons lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability despite stochastic decoding. Cartridges is evaluated on 20 QuALITY articles while other methods use 50; Appendix B.2 reports original-cache accuracies of 75.0% and 72.1% on these respective sets. Direct comparisons on the same subset, with uncertainty estimated at the context level, are needed to substantiate smaller differences and precise quality-ranking claims.

Attribution and calibration: Nonuniform head budgets are the strongest component in Figure 4, but the manuscript does not clearly identify a held-out calibration/evaluation split for learning these budgets or report the one-time calibration cost. Consequently, the claimed reusable, input-independent schedule is less firmly established than the main compaction results. A matched-budget comparison giving pruning baselines the same learned allocation would better isolate the benefit of attention and value fitting.

Systems significance is only partially demonstrated: The paper measures compaction time but does not establish end-to-end decoding latency, throughput, peak working memory, or the amortization point for compaction. These measurements matter because reference-query generation and fitting consume resources, and efficient nonuniform caches require suitable kernels. Gemma’s reported ratios cover only global-attention layers, as the authors disclose, so they are not total-cache reduction factors. The extrapolation to much larger models based primarily on KV-cache dimensions also overlooks the cost of generating reference queries.

Reproducibility and presentation details need correction: Algorithm 2 loops t times while selecting k keys per iteration, which would select kt keys rather than the stated budget t unless an unstated stopping condition is applied. Algorithm 1’s unnormalized correlation rule does not generally select the column giving the greatest residual reduction, contrary to the accompanying description. Together with unspecified budget-calibration details and no provided implementation link, these issues make exact reproduction harder. They appear repairable and do not invalidate the central empirical contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The central formulation is well motivated. Matching both local attention outputs and attention mass preserves a compacted block’s contribution when concatenated with other tokens, for queries where matching holds (Section 2; Appendix A). The scalar biases directly address the mass lost through token removal.

Originality: The contribution is a useful combination of attention-behavior matching, mass-correcting biases, and inexpensive value fitting. Although least squares, OMP, reconstruction queries, and nonuniform budgets are established ingredients, their integration provides a meaningful alternative to end-to-end latent-cache optimization.

Significance: Figure 3 shows substantial improvements over pruning and summarization across three model families and two comprehension benchmarks, particularly at aggressive compaction ratios. Figure 1 demonstrates an attractive quality–compaction-time tradeoff relative to the evaluated Cartridges configuration.

Experimental analysis: Ablations examine biases, fitted values, head budgets, query sources, and on-policy extraction. The supplementary reasoning experiment also provides preliminary evidence that repeated compaction can preserve useful state.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main explanation is clear, and the appendices provide prompts, model identifiers, dataset selection, baseline adaptations, numerical procedures, and pseudocode. The limitations discussion candidly acknowledges slower variants, weaker results at extreme compaction, and unfinished inference-engine integration. No material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness of optimization claims: The implementation does not generally solve the stated NNLS problems. Appendix C.2 uses clamped unconstrained least squares for OMP and only two projected-gradient steps for HighestAttnKeys; clipping is not an NNLS solution in general. Thus the claims of closed-form construction and avoiding gradient descent need qualification. In addition, Appendix A.2’s per-query feature rescaling changes the least-squares weighting across queries unless compensated, so the implemented objective should be stated explicitly.

Evaluation uncertainty: Main accuracy curves lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variability despite stochastic decoding. LongHealth contains only four compacted contexts, so 400 questions provide limited evidence of generalization across contexts. Cartridges uses 20 QuALITY articles while the other methods use 50; the reported full-cache accuracies differ by 2.9 percentage points between these sets. Matched-subset comparisons and context-level uncertainty would make superiority claims more convincing.

Reproducibility of the strongest component: Nonuniform head budgets produce the largest ablation benefit, but the manuscript does not clearly identify a disjoint calibration/evaluation split, fully specify sensitivity-curve construction and interpolation, or report calibration cost. Transfer evidence consists largely of selected-head plots. A held-out comparison using a fixed published schedule would strengthen this central result.

Practical significance is narrower than some efficiency claims suggest. There are no end-to-end decoding-throughput, peak-memory, or amortization measurements for the biased, nonuniform cache. Table 1 omits the target compaction ratio, and its 565-second OMP cost exceeds the 139-second self-study cost, contrary to the unqualified statement that query generation dominates runtime. Similar KV sizes alone also do not establish similar total compaction costs for much larger models, because reference-query generation requires model computation.

Algorithm presentation needs correction: Algorithm 2 runs t iterations while adding k keys per iteration, which exceeds the stated budget for k > 1. Algorithm 1’s unnormalized correlation rule does not generally select the column with maximal residual reduction as claimed. These issues are repairable, but obscure precisely which heuristic produced the reported results.

strengths: Soundness: The central formulation is well motivated. Section 2 and Appendix A correctly decompose attention over concatenated blocks into local outputs and attention masses, explaining why both must be preserved. The scalar bias provides a principled correction for the mass lost through token removal.

Significance: The empirical improvements are substantial across three model families and several task types. On QASPER, retaining 5% of the cache achieves F1 of 0.416 versus 0.444 with the original Qwen cache, compared with 0.220 for KVzip (Table 1). On RULER, the fast variant achieves 83.3% versus KVzip’s 46.6% at 5% retention with Llama (Table 11). These results support a useful advance beyond the primary multiple-choice benchmarks.

Originality: Although subset selection, least squares, and OMP are established techniques, combining attention-mass correction with fitted values yields a meaningful new compaction procedure. The contribution includes useful understanding of why preserving locally normalized attention alone is insufficient.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript clearly develops the objective and method variants, and provides substantial implementation detail, prompts, baseline adaptations, and numerical settings. Ablations examine biases, fitted values, head allocation, reference queries, and on-policy extraction.

Limitations: The discussion appropriately acknowledges expensive OMP variants, Cartridges’ advantage at some extreme compaction ratios, restrictions from selecting existing keys, and unfinished inference-engine integration. These qualifications help distinguish demonstrated results from future applications.
weaknesses: Soundness and presentation: The claims of closed-form construction and avoiding gradient descent entirely are inaccurate for the implemented procedure. Appendix C.2 uses clamped unconstrained least squares for OMP and two projected-gradient steps for HighestAttnKeys; neither generally solves the stated NNLS problem exactly. Furthermore, Appendix A.2’s per-query rescaling changes the least-squares weighting across queries, although it preserves the exact matching equations. The manuscript should state the actual approximate, weighted objectives and distinguish them from exact minimization.

Evaluation: Uncertainty is inadequately quantified despite stochastic decoding. LongHealth contains only four independent contexts, while LongBench v2 uses 47 examples selected according to full-context/no-context correctness. The latter is a useful conditional diagnostic, but does not establish performance on the overall benchmark. Repeated runs and confidence intervals clustered by context would make close comparisons more credible.

Baseline comparability: Cartridges is evaluated on 20 QuALITY contexts while other methods use 50. Appendix B.2 reports original-cache accuracy of 75.0% on the smaller subset versus 71.1% overall, which is not negligible relative to several plotted differences. Reporting all methods on the common subset would strengthen the headline Cartridges comparison. Adapted question-agnostic SnapKV and PyramidKV results should also remain clearly distinguished from their original operating settings.

Systems significance: Reduced stored KV size and compaction timings do not establish end-to-end serving benefits. There are no measured decode-throughput results, peak compaction memory measurements, or amortization analyses for the biased, nonuniform cache. Table 3 omits the target retention ratio, although OMP cost depends on it. Extrapolating efficiency to much larger models from KV dimensions alone also overlooks query generation, which the paper identifies as a major runtime component.

Reproducibility: Some consequential details remain incomplete. The calibration/evaluation separation and construction cost for precomputed head budgets are unclear. Algorithm 2 loops t times while adding k keys each time, apparently exceeding its stated budget when k > 1. Explicit budget enforcement, calibration splits, decoding settings, seeds, and executable configurations would improve independent reproducibility.

Research ethics: No material ethical violation is evident, but Appendix G.1 overstates the safety evidence. Ordinary QA and reconstruction metrics do not ensure that alignment or instruction-following degradation would be detected, and qualitative missing-information examples do not establish a generally low-risk failure mode. These claims should be narrowed or supported with targeted evaluations.

strengths: Soundness: The central decomposition is correct and useful: preserving both local attention outputs and attention mass preserves a block’s contribution when combined with other tokens (Appendix A.2). The scalar biases address a real deficiency of unweighted token eviction, and fitting values by least squares is well motivated.

Significance: The empirical improvements are substantial across comprehension, generative QA, and retrieval. On QASPER at 2% retained cache, AM achieves 0.373 versus KVzip’s 0.124 for Qwen, and 0.387 versus 0.104 for Llama (Table 1). On RULER, the fast variant achieves 83.3% versus 46.6% for KVzip at 5% retained cache on Llama (Table 11). These results support a useful contribution beyond the headline experiment.

Originality: Although least squares, OMP, and attention-based selection are established tools, their combination around mass-preserving attention matching provides a meaningful new formulation for post-hoc KV compaction without model finetuning.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript clearly separates reference-query generation, key selection, mass fitting, and value fitting. Appendices provide prompts, solver details, baseline adaptations, and dataset selection procedures. Ablations examine the principal components rather than reporting only aggregate improvements.

Limitations: The paper appropriately acknowledges slow OMP variants, weaker performance than Cartridges in some extreme-compaction settings, and unfinished serving-engine integration. The breadth and magnitude of the measured improvements justify acceptance despite the qualifications below.
weaknesses: Optimization claims exceed the implementation. Section 3 describes closed-form construction and avoiding gradient descent, but Appendix C.2 uses projected gradient descent for HighestAttnKeys and clipped unconstrained least squares for OMP. Clipping does not generally solve NNLS. Appendix A’s per-query rescaling also changes the least-squares weighting across queries. The actual approximate objective and solver should be stated consistently. Algorithm 2 additionally loops t times while selecting k keys per iteration, contradicting its stated budget t when k > 1.

Statistical and comparison limitations weaken precise rankings. Most downstream results lack uncertainty estimates despite stochastic decoding. LongHealth contains only four aggregated contexts. Cartridges is evaluated on 20 QuALITY articles whereas other methods use 50; Appendix B.2 reports full-cache accuracies of 75.0% and 71.1% respectively. A paired comparison on the same articles is needed to substantiate the exact quality advantage over Cartridges.

LongBench v2 evaluates only 47 contexts selected using full-context and no-context outcomes. Re-evaluating all methods makes the conditional comparison informative, but it does not establish performance on the complete benchmark or its individual domains.

Deployment efficiency remains incompletely established. Compaction timings do not demonstrate end-to-end decoding throughput, peak working memory, or amortization across requests. Nonuniform budgets and per-token biases require practical kernel support. The extrapolation to much larger models based on KV size is particularly uncertain because query generation also depends on model compute. The calibration cost and exact reusable head-budget artifacts are insufficiently specified.

Generalization and ethics claims need narrower wording. Matching sampled reference queries provides no general guarantee for unseen queries or accumulated multilayer errors. Appendix G.1’s assertion that QA and reconstruction metrics would expose any instruction-following degradation is unsupported; these metrics do not constitute an alignment evaluation. Likewise, describing observed information omissions as a generally low-risk failure mode goes beyond the evidence, especially for clinical-document applications.

strengths: Soundness: The core formulation is well motivated. Section 2 and Appendix A correctly explain why preserving both local attention outputs and attention mass preserves a compacted block’s contribution under concatenation, for matched queries. The scalar biases address a real deficiency of unweighted token eviction, and fitting values by least squares follows naturally.

Significance: The empirical improvements are substantial and extend beyond one benchmark. On QASPER, Llama retains 0.436 F1 versus 0.456 with the full cache at 5% retained size, compared with 0.301 for H2O+ and 0.168 for KVzip. On RULER, the fast variant achieves 83.3% versus KVzip’s 46.6% at 5% retained size for Llama. These results support a useful advance in aggressive, question-agnostic cache compaction.

Originality: The contribution combines established numerical tools into a distinctive attention-preserving compaction objective. Matching attention mass explicitly, fitting retained values, and using reference queries provides useful understanding beyond another token-importance heuristic. The nonuniform allocation and on-policy query experiments further clarify which design choices matter.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally clear, with informative ablations and extensive implementation details covering prompts, solver settings, precision, baseline adaptations, and positional handling. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges OMP cost, restricted key selection, Cartridges’ advantages at extreme ratios, and unfinished serving integration.
weaknesses: Soundness and algorithmic precision: Claims that construction is entirely closed-form and avoids gradient descent are overstated. Appendix C.2 uses clamped unconstrained least squares for OMP and two projected-gradient steps for HighestAttnKeys; neither generally solves NNLS exactly. Appendix A’s per-query rescaling also changes the weighting of the stated least-squares objective. These approximations should be reflected in the main formulation and validated through residual or solver-sensitivity measurements. Algorithm 2 additionally selects k keys for each of t iterations despite specifying a budget of t.

Evaluation uncertainty: Main accuracy results lack confidence intervals or repeated-run estimates despite sampled decoding. LongHealth contains only four independent contexts, and LongBench v2 uses a selected 47-context subset, so those results establish narrower generalization than an unfiltered benchmark evaluation. Cartridges is evaluated on 20 QuALITY contexts while other methods use 50; Appendix B.2 reports full-cache accuracies of 75.0% and 71.1% respectively. A paired comparison on the same contexts is needed to substantiate precise superiority claims.

Systems significance: Compaction timings demonstrate a useful speed advantage, but actual serving benefits remain unmeasured. There are no end-to-end decode-throughput, peak-memory, or amortization measurements with biased, nonuniform caches. Table 3 omits the target compaction ratio, although OMP cost depends strongly on retained size. Extrapolating runtime to much larger models from KV dimensions alone overlooks reference-query generation cost.

Reproducibility and attribution: The model-specific head budgets are particularly important in Figure 5, yet the calibration procedure does not clearly identify a held-out calibration split, all allocation settings, or its total cost. Providing the resulting schedules and clarifying separation from evaluation contexts would strengthen reproducibility and the claimed transferability of these budgets.

Research ethics and limitations: No material ethical barrier to acceptance is evident, but Appendix G.1 overstates what ordinary QA and reconstruction metrics establish about alignment and instruction following. Keeping system tokens unchanged does not ensure their behavioral influence survives compaction. The claim of a graceful, low-risk failure mode should be qualified or supported by targeted evaluation.
